title: Metric & Imperial Conversion
keyIdea: Metric units (centimetres, kilograms, litres) and imperial units (inches, pounds, pints) measure the same things in different-sized steps. Rough rules are enough for everyday estimates: 1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm (exactly 2.54), 1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds, and 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints (a UK pint is 568 ml). To convert, multiply or divide by the rule. Ask whether the new unit is smaller or bigger: changing to a smaller unit gives a bigger number, so multiply (4 inches ≈ 4 × 2.5 = 10 cm); changing to a bigger unit gives a smaller number, so divide (7 pounds ≈ 7 ÷ 2.2 ≈ 3 kg). Always check the answer makes sense.
familyTip: Hunt for imperial units at home or in a shop: a pint of milk, a TV size in inches, a recipe in pounds. Estimate each one in metric units together, then check with a ruler, scales or a jug.

visual.caption: Is each rough rule about right or way off? Drag each card to a box, or tap it and then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: stretch a pencil along a cm and inch ruler, balance 5 kg with pound weights, pour pints into 4 litres, sort × or ÷, estimate.

kid: There are two big families of units. Metric units are centimetres, kilograms and litres. Imperial units are older: inches, pounds and pints. In the UK you still see both. A TV is sold in inches, a baby's weight is often told in pounds, and milk comes in pints.

An inch is longer than a centimetre. About 2.5 centimetres fit along one inch, so 4 inches is about 10 cm, and 12 inches (one foot) is about 30 cm. A kilogram is heavier than a pound: 1 kg is about 2.2 pounds. A litre is more than a pint: 1 litre is about 1.75 pints.

To convert, multiply or divide by the rule. First ask: is the new unit smaller or bigger? If it is smaller, you need more of them, so multiply. 6 inches is about 6 × 2.5 = 15 cm. If it is bigger, you need fewer of them, so divide. 22 pounds is about 22 ÷ 2.2 = 10 kg.

These rules are rough, but they are good for estimates. A new baby of 7 pounds is about 3 kg. A 12-inch pizza is about 30 cm across. Always check that your answer makes sense. A baby of 15 kg would be far too heavy!
adult: Ages 9 to 10. This matches the National Curriculum in England for Year 5 measurement: understand and use approximate equivalences between metric units and common imperial units such as inches, pounds and pints. It leads to Year 6 converting between miles and kilometres. Exact values are from the UK Weights and Measures Act 1985 and NIST: 1 inch = 2.54 cm, 1 pound = 0.45359237 kg, 1 UK pint = 568.26 ml.

The lab has five tasks. Learners stretch a pencil along a ruler marked in cm and inches to 4 inches, about 20 cm and 1 foot. They balance a 5 kg bag with eleven 1 lb weights. They pour UK pints into a 4-litre bucket and find it takes seven. Then they sort six conversions into × 2.5, ÷ 2.5, × 2.2 or ÷ 2.2, and estimate a baby's weight, a pizza and a jug on number lines.

Common mistakes. Pupils often multiply when they should divide, giving a 7-pound baby as 15 kg. Some think the number stays the same across units, or add the rule instead of multiplying. Many flip the rule and say 1 pound is 2.2 kg. Ask: is the new unit bigger or smaller, so should the number go up or down? Be careful with pints: a US pint is smaller, about 473 ml.

practice.hint: Look at the double ruler: which marks are further apart?
practice.explain: An inch is about 2.5 cm, so it is longer than a centimetre. That is why inch numbers are smaller.

practice.prompt: A pencil is {n} inches long. About how many centimetres is that? (1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm)
practice.hint: Centimetres are smaller, so there will be more of them: multiply.
practice.explain: {n} × 2.5 = {=n*2.5} cm. Changing to the smaller unit gives the bigger number.

practice.prompt: A new baby weighs 7 pounds. About how much is that in kilograms?
practice.hint: Kilograms are heavier than pounds, so there will be fewer of them.
practice.explain: 7 ÷ 2.2 is about 3, so the baby is about 3 kg. 15 kg came from multiplying, which goes the wrong way.

practice.prompt: A bag of potatoes weighs {n} kg. About how many pounds is that? (1 kg ≈ 2.2 pounds)
practice.hint: Pounds are lighter, so you need more of them: multiply by 2.2.
practice.explain: {n} × 2.2 = {=n*2.2} pounds. More of the smaller unit.

practice.prompt: To change centimetres to inches, you…
practice.hint: Inches are bigger than centimetres. Should the number go up or down?
practice.explain: Inches are the bigger unit, so you need fewer of them: divide by 2.5. For example 50 cm ÷ 2.5 = 20 inches.

pool.prompt: About how many pints are in 1 litre?
pool.hint: Remember the bucket: 7 pints filled 4 litres.
pool.explain: A litre is more than a pint: 1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints, because a UK pint is 568 ml.

pool.prompt: A ribbon is {=n*5} cm long. About how many inches is it? (1 inch ≈ 2.5 cm)
pool.hint: Inches are bigger, so there will be fewer of them: divide by 2.5.
pool.explain: {=n*5} ÷ 2.5 = {=n*2} inches. The bigger unit gives the smaller number.

pool.prompt: Which holds more: a 1-pint bottle or a 1-litre bottle?
pool.hint: A pint is 568 ml. How many ml in a litre?
pool.explain: A litre is 1,000 ml and a pint is 568 ml, so the litre bottle holds more, about 1.75 pints.

pool.prompt: A paddling pool needs {n} litres of water. About how many pints is that? (1 litre ≈ 1.75 pints)
pool.hint: Pints are smaller than litres, so you need more of them: multiply.
pool.explain: {n} × 1.75 = {=n*1.75} pints. More of the smaller unit.

pool.prompt: A dog weighs 22 pounds. About how many kilograms is that?
pool.hint: Divide by 2.2, because kilograms are the bigger unit.
pool.explain: 22 ÷ 2.2 = 10, so the dog is about 10 kg. 48 kg came from multiplying, and 24 kg from adding.

pool.prompt: A TV screen is 40 inches across. Which is the best estimate in centimetres?
pool.hint: Centimetres are smaller, so the number gets bigger: multiply by 2.5.
pool.explain: 40 × 2.5 = 100, so about 100 cm (exactly 101.6 cm). 16 cm came from dividing; 42 cm from adding.

pool.prompt: A suitcase weighs {=n*11} pounds. About how many kilograms is that? (11 pounds ≈ 5 kg)
pool.hint: How many lots of 11 pounds are there? Each lot is about 5 kg.
pool.explain: {=n*11} pounds is {n} lots of 11 pounds, and each is about 5 kg, so {n} × 5 = {=n*5} kg.

pool.prompt: Sam says 5 kg is the same as 5 pounds. What is the best answer?
choices: No: 5 kg is about 11 pounds, because a kilogram is heavier
Yes: the number stays the same
pool.hint: Think of the balance: how many 1 lb weights matched the 5 kg bag?
pool.explain: A kilogram is heavier than a pound, so you need more pounds: 5 × 2.2 = 11 pounds.

pool.prompt: Why do we use 2.5 for inches to centimetres when the exact value is 2.54?
choices: 2.5 is easy to work with and close enough for estimates
pool.hint: Is 4 × 2.5 or 4 × 2.54 easier in your head?
pool.explain: 1 inch is exactly 2.54 cm, but 2.5 is easier and the difference is tiny for estimates: 4 inches is 10 cm or 10.16 cm.
